section_title: What does Paul’s story show about Christ’s mercy?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 12 I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who has strengthened me, that He considered me faithful and appointed me to service. 13 I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man; yet because I had acted in ignorance and unbelief, I was shown mercy. 14 And the grace of our Lord overflowed to me, along with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.

15 This is a trustworthy saying, worthy of full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst. 16 But for this very reason I was shown mercy, so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus might display His perfect patience as an example to those who would believe in Him for eternal life. 17 Now to the King eternal, immortal, and invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

context_lines: After speaking of the gospel entrusted to him, Paul thanks Christ for strengthening him and appointing him to service. He remembers that he had been a blasphemer, a persecutor and a violent man.
He does not hide that past. He says he acted in ignorance and unbelief and received mercy, with the Lord’s grace overflowing in faith and love in Christ Jesus.

The trustworthy message is that Christ came into the world to save sinners. Paul counts himself the worst. The Greek word is protos (PROH-toss); [Thayer’s lexicon](https://biblehub.com/greek/4413.htm) includes first in rank or chief and specifically lists verse 15. His words stress the seriousness of his sin and the greatness of the mercy shown to him.

Paul then states why his case matters to others: Christ’s patience toward him provides an example for those who will believe for eternal life. His account ends in praise to the eternal, immortal and invisible God.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly understand this as testimony to Christ’s mercy toward a former persecutor and encouragement to sinners who hear the gospel. [Wesley’s notes on verses 12–17](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-first-epistle-to-timothy/) emphasize abundant grace and hope for others. The [USCCB note](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/1timothy/1) likewise connects Paul’s experience with Jesus’ saving purpose and the praise it produces. Paul’s past is evidence of the mercy he received, rather than a reason to minimize his wrongs.
god_plan_lines: [Acts 9:10–16](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/9.htm) gives the striking setting: the man feared for harming believers is appointed to carry Jesus’ name to others. Mercy makes a former persecutor a servant of the message he opposed.

[Titus 2:11–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/titus/2.htm) connects the appearing of saving grace with Christ’s purpose of redeeming a people for Himself and teaching them a new way of life as they await His glory. Paul’s story displays that work in a particular person, with a purpose that reaches those who will believe after him.
